title: Ashoka's Pillars in Nepal: Lumbini, Niglihawa, Gotihawa
meta_description: The Ashoka pillars of Nepal: what the Lumbini and Niglihawa inscriptions say, the broken stump at Gotihawa, how they were found and how to visit all three.
summary: Emperor Ashoka raised stone pillars at sacred Buddhist sites in the third century BCE, and three stand in Nepal: the inscribed pillar at Lumbini naming the Buddha's birthplace, the broken inscribed pillar at Niglihawa and a stump at Gotihawa. All three can be seen in a day and a half from Lumbini.

sections.heading: Who Ashoka was
paras: Ashoka ruled the Maurya empire from its capital Pataliputra, near modern Patna in India, in the third century BCE, over most of the subcontinent. Early in his reign he conquered Kalinga, on India's east coast, in a war his own inscriptions describe with remorse: they speak of a hundred and fifty thousand people carried away and many more killed. After it he turned to the Buddha's teaching and to what he called dhamma, a public ethic of non-violence, tolerance and care for people and animals.

He spread that message in writing. Ashoka's edicts, carved on rock faces and on polished stone pillars across his empire, are the earliest substantial body of written records from South Asia that survive. Most are in Prakrit languages written in Brahmi script; in the far north-west some are in Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic. Brahmi was deciphered by James Prinsep in the 1830s, and once it could be read, these inscriptions changed the study of early Indian history.

The pillars themselves are single shafts of fine sandstone, many quarried at Chunar near Varanasi and polished to a glassy shine, then moved hundreds of kilometres. Many carried animal capitals, the most famous being the lion capital of Sarnath, now the national emblem of India.

sections.heading: The pilgrimage of the twentieth year
paras: Two of Nepal's pillars carry inscriptions dated to the twentieth year after Ashoka's consecration, around 249 BCE. They record that the king came in person, worshipped, and set up a stone pillar. Together they show an emperor travelling to the places linked to the Buddha and to the Buddhas believed to have come before him, and marking each with a monument.

Later Buddhist literature adds a legend. The Ashokavadana, a Sanskrit text composed centuries afterwards, says that the elder monk Upagupta guided the king from site to site, telling him at each one what had happened there. At Lumbini, the story goes, Upagupta stretched out his hand and said that here the Blessed One was born. The text is a work of devotion rather than history, but it shows how early the idea of a pilgrimage route to the Buddha's places took hold.

sections.heading: The Lumbini pillar
paras: The best-known pillar stands beside the Maya Devi Temple in the Sacred Garden. Its inscription, in five lines of Brahmi, says that King Devanampiya Piyadasi, Ashoka's royal title, came here himself in the twentieth year of his reign and worshipped because the Buddha Shakyamuni was born here. He caused a stone wall or stone figure to be made, the meaning of one word is still debated, and a stone pillar set up to show that the Blessed One was born here. He made the village of Lumbini free of tax and liable to pay only one eighth of its produce.

That tax exemption is a detail that matters. It is a practical, administrative act, the sort of thing a government records, and it ties the inscription firmly to this village. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited in the seventh century, described a pillar here with the figure of a horse on top, split down the middle by lightning. The capital is now lost.

The pillar lay buried and forgotten for centuries. In December 1896 an expedition involving the German archaeologist Alois Anton Führer and Khadga Shumsher Rana, governor of Palpa, uncovered the inscription. It is the main evidence by which the birthplace was identified, and the oldest dated inscription found in Nepal.

sections.heading: Niglihawa and the Buddha Konakamana
paras: About 25–30 km west of Lumbini, near Taulihawa in Kapilvastu district, the village of Niglihawa has a broken Ashoka pillar beside a large pond known as Nigali Sagar. The shaft lies in two pieces, the upper part on the ground and the lower part standing in the earth. It was located by Führer in 1895, the year before the Lumbini discovery.

Its inscription records that Ashoka, in the fourteenth year of his reign, enlarged the stupa of the Buddha Konakamana to twice its size, and that in the twentieth year he came himself, worshipped and set up a stone pillar. Konakamana, also called Kanakamuni, is one of the Buddhas who in Buddhist tradition taught in earlier ages before Gautama. The inscription shows that the cult of past Buddhas was already established in Ashoka's time. The pillar also carries much later writing, including an inscription of the fourteenth-century western Nepal king Ripu Malla, a sign that pilgrims still came here 1,500 years after Ashoka.

sections.heading: Gotihawa and the Buddha Krakuchchhanda
paras: Gotihawa, a few kilometres south-west of Taulihawa, has the stump of an Ashoka pillar, the lower part of the shaft standing in a shallow pit, with no inscription surviving. Nearby is the brick base of a stupa. Tradition and the accounts of the Chinese pilgrims link the place with Krakuchchhanda, another Buddha of an earlier age, said to have been born and to have died near here.

Gotihawa is the least visited of the three and the most rural. There is little to see beyond the stump and the mound, but the setting among fields, with farmers working around a monument raised by an emperor 2,200 years ago, is part of its pull.

sections.heading: Ashoka and the stupa at Ramagrama
paras: Ashoka's name in Nepal is tied to one more site, though it has no pillar. After the Buddha's death at Kushinagar, the texts say, his relics were divided into eight shares and enshrined in eight stupas by the peoples who claimed them. One share went to the Koliyas of Ramagrama, on the plains east of Lumbini.

Buddhist legend says that Ashoka later opened the original relic stupas to divide the relics again among 84,000 new stupas across his empire. At Ramagrama he was stopped: the stupa was guarded by nagas, serpent beings, who worshipped the relics themselves, and the king left it untouched. For this reason Ramagrama, near Parasi in Nawalparasi district, is honoured as the one relic stupa of the eight that was never opened. Today it is a grassy brick mound on the bank of the Jharahi river, an easy half day from Lumbini, and a fitting place to end a journey in Ashoka's footsteps.

sections.heading: Seeing all three
paras: Spend one afternoon in the Sacred Garden at Lumbini, then a full day west to Tilaurakot with Niglihawa, Gotihawa and Kudan. The pillars are fenced or railed; do not climb on them, touch the inscriptions or leave stickers and offerings on the stone itself. Pilgrims leave flowers and lamps at the base instead.

Bring a hat and water; the Kapilavastu sites are open fields with little shade, and from April to June the heat by noon is severe. Our three-night Kapilavastu circuit is built around exactly this route.

faqs.q: How many Ashoka pillars are there in Nepal?
faqs.a: Three are visited in Nepal, all on the plains of Lumbini Province: the inscribed pillar in the Sacred Garden at Lumbini, the broken inscribed pillar at Niglihawa, and an uninscribed stump at Gotihawa, both near Taulihawa in Kapilvastu district. All three are linked to Buddhas: Gautama at Lumbini, and the earlier Buddhas Konakamana and Krakuchchhanda at the other two.

faqs.q: What does the Lumbini pillar inscription say?
faqs.a: It records that King Devanampiya Piyadasi, Ashoka, came in person in the twentieth year of his reign and worshipped because the Buddha Shakyamuni was born here. He set up a stone pillar to mark the birthplace and made the village of Lumbini free of tax, paying only an eighth share of its produce.

faqs.q: When was the Lumbini pillar discovered?
faqs.a: It was uncovered in December 1896 by an expedition involving the German archaeologist Alois Anton Führer and Khadga Shumsher Rana, then governor of Palpa. The pillar had been buried and forgotten for centuries. Its inscription confirmed the site as the birthplace of the Buddha, and it remains the key evidence for Lumbini's identification.

In Buddhist tradition, Konakamana, also called Kanakamuni, is one of the Buddhas who taught in an earlier age, before Gautama. Ashoka's pillar at Niglihawa records that he enlarged Konakamana's stupa to twice its size and later visited it, showing that devotion to past Buddhas was already established in the third century BCE.

faqs.q: Where is Niglihawa and how do I get there?
faqs.a: Niglihawa is a village near Taulihawa in Kapilvastu district, about 25–30 km west of Lumbini, roughly an hour by car. It is usually visited in a day trip with Tilaurakot, Kudan and Gotihawa. Roads are narrow and the last stretch is rural; a hired car with a driver who knows the area is the easiest option.

faqs.q: What language are Ashoka's inscriptions in?
faqs.a: The Nepal inscriptions are in a Prakrit language, a vernacular related to Sanskrit, written in the Brahmi script. Brahmi is the ancestor of most scripts used in South Asia today, including Devanagari, in which Nepali is written. It was deciphered by James Prinsep in the 1830s, which made Ashoka's inscriptions readable again.

faqs.q: Why did the Lumbini pillar have a horse on top?
faqs.a: The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited in the seventh century, described a horse figure on top of the pillar, and said it had been split by lightning. One word in Ashoka's inscription has also been read by some scholars as referring to a stone horse. The capital is lost; only the shaft survives.

faqs.q: Can I touch the Ashoka pillars?
faqs.a: No. The Lumbini pillar is fenced and the inscription is protected; the Niglihawa and Gotihawa pillars are railed or in protected pits. Touching, climbing or sticking offerings on the stone damages it. Pilgrims leave flowers, incense and lamps at the base, and that is the respectful way to make an offering.

If you are already going to Tilaurakot, yes: it is only a short drive, and seeing an Ashoka pillar in a working field gives a sense of how these monuments sat in the landscape. There is little else there beyond the stump and a stupa mound, so if time is short, prioritise Tilaurakot and Niglihawa.
